title: Multi-Domain Transferable Graph Gluing
one_liner: Merge graphs from different domains into one smooth surface so a model trained on all of them transfers better to new domains.
lead: When you train a graph model on data from many different domains (biology graphs, social networks, recommendation systems), the model learns patterns from all of them. But mixing domains can backfire—a pattern useful for biology graphs might be harmful for social networks because they have fundamentally different structures. This paper offers a new answer: think of each domain's graphs as living on their own bumpy surface with its own shape. If you can smooth and glue these surfaces together into one coherent whole, the model can learn one consistent rule that works across all of them, because it's learning rules that respect the shared smooth structure, not rules tied to any one domain's quirks.

problem.h2: Why multi-domain graph training doesn't just work
paras: Imagine you have social networks (who follows whom), protein interaction graphs (which proteins bind), and product-recommendation graphs (who buys what). A naive approach trains one model on all three at once. But the model sees contradictory patterns: a connection that means friendship in one domain means protein interaction in another. The model gets confused and forgets how to handle each domain.

A beginner might try: train separate models for each domain, then glue their final learned weights together. This fails because the weights from domain A are tuned to domain A's specific structure—how that domain's graphs cluster and connect. Forcing them to agree with domain B's weights erases the domain-specific knowledge, and the model performs worse on all domains.

callout.html: We don't know how to combine knowledge from different graph domains so models learn one rule that works everywhere without forgetting what makes each domain unique.

steps.text: For each graph, measure its local structure (how things cluster nearby) using adaptive orthogonal frames.
Glue adjacent local geometries smoothly so there are no seams or jumps between regions.
Pre-train the model on the stitched surface to predict graph tasks, learning one consistent rule across all domains.
Calculate how smoothly the manifold connects, which predicts whether a new domain will transfer well.
The model carries the learned rule to new domains that fit the same smooth structure.

paras: The paper changes how the model represents the space it learns in. Instead of learning separate representations for each domain that might clash, it learns a shared structure—the way nodes cluster and connect in each domain, plus how those clusters relate to each other. By making this shared structure smooth and continuous (no sudden jumps or cliffs), the model learns patterns that work across all domains because they rest on consistent rules underneath.
object.object: Geometric structure of the learning space

hidden.h2: Geometric consistency: the quantity that predicts transfer
hidden.name: Geometric consistency score
paras: The paper introduces and measures a hidden quantity: geometric consistency. This is a number that says how smoothly the stitched manifold connects — high consistency means no bumps or jumps where domains meet, low consistency means they clash. You calculate it by checking: if you move a tiny step in one domain's space, do you land in a sensible place in an adjacent domain's space, or do you fall off a cliff?

The paper uses this geometric consistency score to predict transferability without running full experiments. If two domains' local geometries stitch together smoothly, the model will transfer between them. If they clash, it won't. This turns geometric smoothness from an intuition into a measurable quantity.

heat.caption: Darker cells mean smoother local structure and seams; bright cells mean rough transitions where transfer fails.

reads.html: Think of it like gluing three rubber sheets together. If you glue them smoothly (no wrinkles at the seams), a marble can roll from one sheet to the next without bouncing. If you glue them with gaps, the marble gets stuck. Geometric consistency measures how well the gluing worked.

The paper estimates geometric consistency by computing the geodesic distances and curvature at domain boundaries using adaptive orthogonal frames. A low consistency score flags domains that will interfere during transfer.

mechanism.h2: Why stitching domains into a smooth manifold fixes transfer
paras: The core mechanism is simple: if each domain lives on its own bumpy surface, a model trained on that surface learns rules specific to that shape. When you move to a new domain with a different shape, those rules break—the model was learning the surface itself, not universal principles. But if you first glue all domains' surfaces into one smooth, coherent surface using orthogonal frames to match how each domain's graphs cluster locally, then train on that unified surface, the model learns rules that work because they rest on shared structure. A rule learned on a smooth surface transfers, because any new domain with similar clustering patterns can use that rule.

The adaptive orthogonal frames are the technical key: they capture how each domain's local neighborhood is oriented (which directions matter, which are noise). When you align these frames across domains and stitch the local pieces smoothly, you're ensuring that the model sees consistent directions and relationships. No sudden changes in orientation mean no sudden changes in what the model learns.

stages.s: Measure how each domain clusters using aligned directional frames
Stitch local geometries into smooth unified manifold
Pre-train model to predict graph tasks on unified surface
Transferable model that works across domains

math.words: Gluing loss equals the domain pre-training error plus a penalty for rough seams, scaled by geometric consistency
symbols: Total loss for the glued manifold
Prediction error on the pre-training task (e.g., node classification)
Weight controlling how much to penalize rough seams
Geometric consistency at a domain seam (0=rough, 1=smooth)
Slope of the model's output at the seam boundary
Sum over all places where domains meet

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say two domains meet at a seam with consistency C_seam = 0.8 (fairly smooth).
The pre-training loss is L_pretrain = 2.5 (model predicts reasonably well).
The gradient at the seam is ||gradient_seam||^2 = 4.0 (steep slope).
With lambda = 5, the roughness penalty is: (1 - 0.8) * 4.0 = 0.2 * 4.0 = 0.8.
If the seam were rougher (C_seam = 0.5), the penalty would be (1 - 0.5) * 4.0 * 5 = 10.0, making the total much higher.
The model learns to smooth seams because smoother seams have lower loss.

math.note: The loss pushes the model to learn rules that don't change suddenly at domain boundaries, so rules learned in one domain work in another.

charts.title: Naive domain merging
charts.note: Forcing weights to agree erases domain-specific knowledge; all domains suffer.

charts.title: GraphGlue manifold stitching
charts.note: Smooth geometric structure lets each domain keep its knowledge while sharing transfer rules.

items.html: If two domains have fundamentally different graph structures (one is dense, one is sparse; one is tree-like, one is cyclic), no amount of stitching makes them cohere smoothly. The shared surface develops tears, and transfer fails. The method works best when domains are related (same family of tasks).

items.b: Overfitting the gluing to training domains.
items.html: The model can learn to stitch the training domains perfectly while making the shared surface uninviting to new domains. If you use too strong a gluing penalty, you're optimizing for the training domains, not general transfer, because the penalty becomes so large it forces the surface to bend to match the training data exactly. The geometric consistency score helps: it measures how smoothly the local directional frames align, and that score only stays high if the surface truly curves smoothly in consistent ways (not if it is just bent to fit the data). You must still validate on held-out domains to prove that transfer actually works, because overfitting can hide even from the consistency score.

items.b: Directional frames fail on flat graphs.
items.html: If a domain's graph is nearly flat or all nodes are nearly identical, the adaptive orthogonal frames cannot reliably measure local structure. The stitching becomes arbitrary, and transfer breaks.

Choose domains that share some structural similarity (all social graphs, or all recommendation graphs). Validate the geometric consistency score on held-out domains to ensure it predicts transfer. Use moderate gluing penalties to balance domain cohesion with transfer readiness.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small experiment with three synthetic graph domains: one social-network-like (nodes are people, edges are friendships), one biological (nodes are proteins, edges are interactions), and one recommendation-like (nodes are users and items, edges are purchases). Pre-train a graph model on all three using manifold gluing. Then measure transfer: take a new held-out domain similar to each, and measure how well the pre-trained model performs without fine-tuning. Compare it to a model trained naively on just the training domains, and to a model trained only on one domain. The glued model should transfer better because it learned rules on a smooth unified surface.
demo.metric_eq: Transfer gain = (glued model accuracy on new domain) - (single-domain model accuracy on new domain)
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss: models trained on smoothly stitched structures transfer to new domains better than models trained on jumbled domains, because the smooth structure forces the model to learn rules that do not depend on any one domain's peculiar shape, and those rules generalize to new domains with similar structure.
